On the contrary, it achieves it almost automatically, through the simple description of the phenomenological aspect of dialectical reality.

If we begin correctly, describe that beginning correctly, and then correctly describe each dialectical transformation of what is being described, the description will of itself return to its starting point.
We can even say that the choice of starting point is indifferent.
A phenomenological investigation can begin with any phenomenon.
If that phenomenon is not original, an analysis of its dialectical structure will reveal this and force us, before moving “forward,” to search for its dialectical “sources.”
Ultimately this search will lead us to the true beginning of Phenomenology.

Indeed, one could say that the phenomenologist begins his investigation from the end of Phenomenology, since in fact he begins from his own existence as a phenomenologist and searches for its dialectical premises.
But in a systematic exposition, Phenomenology must begin “at the beginning.”

Its starting point must therefore be the original “birth” of humanity: the first thesis, still purely natural, in which negativity appeared for the first time and thereby transformed that thesis into the first antithesis, which was already human.
And we will see that this “appearance” is indeed the point from which Phenomenology begins.
Viewed from its theoretical side, this phenomenon is called sensation.
Viewed from its practical or active side, it is called desire.

Starting from this beginning—from this “desiring sensation” or “sensing desire”—and describing all its dialectical transformations correctly, phenomenological description will, so to speak, return to it automatically.

But before explaining how this return occurs, how the description leads us back to the beginning, and what that return means, we must first pause over an essential difference between Hegel’s Phenomenology and my own.
For Hegel, his system was true in the strong sense.
He regarded it as the system of definitive or “perfect” knowledge—in other words, as wisdom.
His Phenomenology therefore appeared to him as definitive.
He could think this only because he believed that the real process of humanity’s historical or dialectical development—the process described in his system—had itself been completed.

If history in the proper sense—understood as humanity’s creative sociopolitical activity—has ended, then there really is nothing left to do except describe retrospectively the history that has “appeared” and investigate its cosmological and ontological “causes.”

This is why, once Hegel had reached the description of his own age, he could say that going any “further” could consist only in studying, on the one hand, the “appearances” of past history and, on the other, their “causes”—that is, in writing a Phenomenology and an Encyclopaedia, or what in my terminology would be Phenomenology and Philosophy.

Consequently, when Hegel reaches the end of the Phenomenology and arrives at the description of himself, he can show that nothing remains for him to do except write the Phenomenology—which he has already written.

So if one wants to move “beyond” the final stage described in the book, one must begin reading the book again from the beginning. The “next” historical or dialectical stage is precisely the writing of the Phenomenology, and one can know what this consists in only by reading it.
We, however, as disciples and successors of Marx-Lenin-Stalin, cannot regard history as already complete.
Even if we made the assumption—factually false—that socialism had been fully realized throughout the world, communism would still remain to be realized.
Creative-and-revolutionary activity is therefore still entirely possible, and the retrospective description of the past is by no means the only thing left to do.
In other words, Phenomenology does not end in the necessary repetition of itself. It ends instead with hypothetical remarks about humanity’s future historical, that is, sociopolitical development.
My Phenomenology, then, is less circular than Hegel’s.
Even so, in principle, it should be just as circular.
When describing any “appearance” or phenomenon, we must distinguish two things.
First, there is the way the appearing reality appears to the consciousness to which it appears—that is, to the consciousness the author of the Phenomenology is describing at a particular stage.
Second, there is the way that same reality is given to the author himself.

Or, as Hegel puts it, we must distinguish between the way a phenomenon exists for the consciousness itself (für das Bewusstsein selbst) and the way it exists for us (für uns)—that is, for the author of the Phenomenology, who in Hegel’s view sees the phenomenon as it truly is, or “in itself” (an sich).
At the beginning of phenomenological description, the standpoint of the consciousness being described and the standpoint of the consciousness doing the describing diverge as widely as possible.
A human being reduced to the standpoint of “desiring sensation” or “sensing desire” speaks about—and describes—themselves in a completely different way from the phenomenologist.
And this very divergence shows the phenomenologist that he cannot stop at this sensation or desire.
There must be other phenomena—or at the very least, this sensation must appear differently to the phenomenologist himself.
In searching for these other phenomena, the phenomenologist finds one in which the divergence is already somewhat smaller, then another in which it is smaller still, and so on.
As he moves from one phenomenon to another, he observes the gradual disappearance of the difference between the consciousness being described and his own consciousness.
Of course, nothing we have just said is new.

By following the order in which the difference between “for a consciousness” and “for us” gradually disappears, the phenomenologist is simply following the path of real dialectical development. The order establishes itself.
The reason is—as we saw earlier—that dialectical overcoming always involves a certain understanding of what has been overcome.

Only by distinguishing the thesis from the antithesis does a human being actually understand the thesis. They take a critical distance from it, see its “limits,” and therefore grasp its determinations.

And because a thesis exposed to dialectical negation is preserved within the synthesis in an “overcome” or “sublated” form, we can say that synthesis is nothing other than the thesis made conscious or understood.
In this sense the thesis has been “raised to a higher level,” since what is conscious in a human being is higher than what remains unconscious or only half-conscious.

This can create the impression that it is precisely the understanding of a given appearance that dialectically “sublates” it, raises it to a higher level, and therefore acts as the driving force of dialectical development.
But this is only an appearance.
It is actually negation that causes the understanding. Negation—negativity, the antithesis—is the true driving force of dialectic.
Still, it remains true that at every dialectical stage the consciousness to which reality appears becomes increasingly developed or complete.
Reality as it appears to that consciousness becomes progressively less different from the reality that is appearing.

And since the phenomenologist’s standpoint is, in principle, philosophical or true—since reality is supposedly given to him as it truly is—the dialectical process appears as a gradual convergence between the standpoints being described and the standpoint of the phenomenologist doing the describing.
This means that Phenomenology has reached its “normal” end and can go no further.
For this coincidence shows that, in the course of his descriptions, the phenomenologist has reached his own standpoint.
If he wishes to continue, he must therefore describe that standpoint itself.
In other words, he must describe the content of the phenomenologist’s consciousness as a phenomenologist.
But the content of that consciousness is nothing other than the Phenomenology itself, since the phenomenologist is its author and, as phenomenologist, nothing more than its author.
The “next” stage of Phenomenology therefore consists in repeating its entire content.
Its end thus returns once more to its beginning.

Through Phenomenology, then, the phenomenologist understands, explains, or deduces himself as the author of the Phenomenology. He shows why the content of his consciousness necessarily belongs to the person he is rather than to someone else.
This is precisely what its circularity consists in.
Here again, however, we must emphasize the difference between Hegel’s Phenomenology and mine.

By understanding himself as a phenomenologist, Hegel found that he could do nothing other than write the Phenomenology and then move from it to the Encyclopaedia—that is, in our terminology, to Philosophy.

When I understand myself in the same way, by contrast, I find myself to be a Marxist-Leninist-Stalinist. For me, alongside the possibility of phenomenological and philosophical knowledge, there still remains the possibility—and indeed the duty—of creative-and-revolutionary sociopolitical activity: the completion of socialism and the laying of the foundations of future communism.
But insofar as I am a phenomenologist, I find myself in the same situation as Hegel.
Within that limit, my Phenomenology is just as circular as his.
Yet this limitation, without destroying the circularity, changes its meaning and importance.
For Hegel, because history had ended, the standpoint of the phenomenologist was in principle absolute.

Reality did not merely “appear” to a consciousness peculiar to the phenomenologist—that is, a consciousness characteristic of his historical age—nor was reality mediated by a form of knowledge that existed only for him.
Reality was supposedly given to him as it truly is.
The Marxist phenomenologist, by contrast, knows that even under fully realized socialism a socialist ideology still prevails, whereas the “true” reveals itself completely only under communism.
In other words, he knows that reality appears to him only in a specifically socialist form.
This means that the end of his Phenomenology is not the end of the definitive Phenomenology.
It is not the final end of the dialectical development of phenomena, or of the ways in which world and humanity appear to human beings.
The reason is simply that human beings themselves are still changing as they pass from socialism to communism.

Even so, the end of a “socialist” Phenomenology is just as necessary and just as much “in the nature of things” as the end of a “communist” Phenomenology, or of the genuinely definitive and fully true Phenomenology.
Once the phenomenologist reaches his own standpoint, he obviously cannot go beyond it.
He must therefore bring his phenomenological description to an end by describing that standpoint—which means, in effect, repeating his own Phenomenology.
In this sense, then, it remains circular.
Phenomenology is circular above all because it eventually reaches the point at which it describes itself and therefore begins to repeat itself.
In this respect, we can say that it is circular in the same way as every complete autobiography.
A genuinely complete autobiography should in principle end with the words:
And to understand fully what that sentence means, one must read the autobiography again.
Only then will we know exactly what the author is doing “now.”
The difference is that an ordinary, non-philosophical autobiography does not demonstrate the necessity of its own being written.
We learn that the author did in fact write it, but we do not see that the author necessarily had to write it.

Phenomenology, by contrast, shows that “now” human beings can in principle do nothing other than write a Phenomenology—at least if they wish to “do” something essentially new, something that did not already exist.
A philosophical or phenomenological autobiography—a Phenomenology—therefore differs from a literary autobiography through its necessity and universality, and hence through its truth.
Yet, as we have seen, all this applies only to the definitive, “communist” Phenomenology.
